_comment: USER-FACING highlights for the release named by `version`, published to the website as
part of https://devicechain.io/releases.json (see hack/build-release-manifest.sh).
🔴 UPDATE THIS IN THE PR THAT PREPARES A RELEASE, BEFORE TAGGING — and update `version`,
`theme`, `breaking` and `highlights` TOGETHER. They are one record of one release, and
the way this file goes wrong is three of the four moving while the fourth keeps last
release's answer: a theme naming work that is not in the highlights below it reads as
confidently as one that is. The `guard` job fails
the release when `version` does not match the tag, deliberately and as the FIRST job —
so a forgotten update costs nothing but a re-run, rather than publishing last release's
highlights against this release's version. Confidently wrong is worse than absent, and
this file is the one part of the manifest a machine cannot derive.
`theme` IS THE ONE PHRASE THAT NAMES THE RELEASE — a chapter title, not a changelog
line. It leads the GitHub release notes and it reaches releases.json, so it is the
first thing a reader decides against. A good one names what changed about the system:
"the instance is declared, not remembered". A bad one is a category ("bug fixes and
improvements"), the version restated, or the first highlight with its verbs filed off —
if it would fit any release, it is not this release's theme.
Write a PHRASE. The guard caps it at 72 characters, the width of a commit subject,
because past that you are writing a sentence, and a sentence about what changed is a
highlight — there is already a list for those below. The cap is the only taste this
file can enforce; the rest is on you.
🔴 The theme is PUBLISHED, and so is every highlight — into the GitHub release body and
into devicechain.io/releases.json. No ADR references in either: ADRs live in a repo the
reader cannot open, so a citation is a dead reference dressed as a source. Say the thing
itself, or link to a public page. THIS BLOCK IS DIFFERENT — `_comment` is published
nowhere, it is the only part of the file a reader never sees, and it may cite ADR-080 or
any other freely. The guard reads exactly that distinction: it scans `theme` and
`highlights[]`, case-insensitively, and leaves this block alone.
WRITE FOR SOMEONE DECIDING WHETHER TO UPGRADE, not for someone reading the commit log.
The changelog is already generated from commit subjects and is right there in the release
notes; repeating `fix(events): give payload rows and anchors identities of their own` here
adds nothing. Say what changed for the person running the platform.
Keep it to a handful of lines. This renders in the website's download menu, not in a
document — a fifteen-item list is a changelog wearing a different hat.
`breaking` MEANS 'THIS RELEASE HAS BREAKING CHANGES'. It does NOT mean 'you must recreate
your instance', and this comment used to say it did — it told you to set the flag when an
upgrade is not a plain `helm upgrade`. The website has not read it that way since the
copy was repaired: `true` renders exactly one sentence, 'This release has breaking changes
— read the release notes before upgrading', and `false` renders nothing at all. So set it
true whenever something breaks for SOMEBODY — an API caller, an operator, a package
consumer — and use the first highlight to say who, and whether the upgrade itself is
ordinary. If a release ever genuinely requires recreating an instance, give that its OWN
manifest field rather than overloading this one a second time.
The other correction: there is no docs banner. Nothing under docs/ fetches releases.json.
The website download menu is this file's only consumer.
For each highlight, ask whether it makes a sentence on the marketing site stale. The
site is a separate repository and nothing here reads its prose. Answering "no site
impact" is a fine answer; not asking is not.
theme: calculated metrics you can author, and an event path that carries more
highlights: Devices must stop sending a credential in the body of an event published over the platform's MQTT broker: such an event is now refused, and a device that was refused should have its credential rotated. A custom C# SDK `IDeviceEventCarrier` must declare the new `CarriesBodyCredential` member or it no longer compiles. Everyone signs in once more after the upgrade, because sign-in state moves to a broker account of its own and the live contents are not carried over. The upgrade from v0.23.0 is in place (`dcctl install`, then `dcctl upgrade`), but it cannot be reached from v0.22.0 or earlier: this release writes events in the compact wire format by default, which those releases cannot read, so upgrade every instance to v0.23.0 first and to v0.24.0 only once every pod runs it. `dcctl` has no option to set the format. The broker moves to NATS 2.15.1 and restarts (twice on the first upgrade that also encrypts the device authentication callout, one server at a time under `--ha`); treat that move as one-way, do not change the broker's replication or restart a broker server by hand while it rolls, and a NATS chart pin below 2.15.0 is now refused. Four migrations add one table and three indexes and rewrite no row. Disabling or deleting a device, or changing a credential, can return `ErrSessionsNotEnded` while `device-management` and `event-sources` run different releases; repeat it once the roll finishes. Other changes to know about: `device` is now a reserved name in calculated-metric formulas (a formula that read a measured metric named `device` as a bare identifier must use `m["device"]`); a calculated value's id changes for a JSON reading that sends no time of its own, so such a reading stored again after the upgrade gets a second derived row; a numeric measurement that is NaN, infinite or 1,000,000,000,000 or more in magnitude is now refused when the event is resolved; DETECT publishes detections 32 at a time by default; `device-management` applies raise-alarm changes on several lanes (6 on the default connection pool); and the MCP endpoint caps a batch at 16 messages and limits each caller to 20 messages a second.

Calculated metrics are authorable end to end: a checked formula editor in the console, per-device numeric constants (`device.calibration`), a formula that reads another calculated metric (chains up to four deep), and a preview of a draft's formulas against a device's stored readings and in detection-rule previews. A new backfill computes a calculated metric for readings stored before its version was published, for up to 90 days and 1,000 devices at a time, and adds only the values that are missing: it needs `device:write` to start or cancel, runs in the background at a bounded rate, and `calculatedBackfill.enabled` turns its worker on, off, or on only when the connection pool has room. Metrics from Sparkplug and LwM2M devices, which send one metric per entry, now compute when they share an instant. Calculated metrics remain off until an operator raises a tier's `calculatedMetricsPerProfile` above 0.

The event path carries more. Events are written in the compact form by default (about a third smaller per message), DETECT overlaps the broker acknowledgements of different devices' detections instead of waiting for each, and raise-alarm changes are applied on several lanes instead of one at a time. On a firing-heavy test load of about 2,500 detections a second offered, a window of 32 published 2,441 detections a second against 528 for the old serial default, and the watermark lag was 5.1 s instead of 139 s.

Two places where a secret rested where every platform service could read it are closed. A device's credential no longer travels in the body of an MQTT event, so it is no longer written into the broker's streams; revoking a credential or disabling a device now also ends the device's open MQTT sessions, and a session ends with its credential. The device authentication callout is encrypted, and the sign-in state (refresh tokens, authorization codes, single sign-on records) lives in a broker account that only user-management can enter.

MQTT fail-closed acknowledgement can now be turned on, and is still off by default. With `infrastructure.nats.mqttFailClosed` on, a QoS 1 PUBACK means the platform holds the message: the broker's message store refuses publishes when full instead of discarding acknowledged ones, devices are backed off before it fills, and `event-sources` forwards what the store holds. Nothing changes unless you set it, and a broker crash with a large backlog is not covered. Separately, on a new install the broker's MQTT gateway streams no longer stay unbounded until `event-sources` restarts, and a new alert, `MqttGatewayStreamUnbounded`, fires when one cannot be bounded.

Dashboards gain widgets: alarm tabs per device type, a trend sparkline and fleet count on the stat card, an alarm severity breakdown, alarm and command markers on the timeseries chart, a one-line-per-device compare chart, and a board drafted from a device type's profile. Saved dashboards render as before.

Smaller changes: the default GKE reference services pool is `t2d-standard-4`, `dcctl upgrade` checks the object-store mount before recording the new version, rule-health counters are written off the detection loop, the detection dashboard gains a rule-health write panel, and the C# SDK builds with a pinned .NET SDK.
